title: Max Posch
text:
I am a Lecturer (Assistant Professor) in the Department of Economics, University of Exeter. My other affiliations include: research associate at Harvard University’s Culture, Cognition, Coevolution Lab, and affiliate fellow at the University of Chicago Booth School of Business’s Stigler Center. I hold a PhD in economics from the University of Zurich.
I study how culture and institutions shape economic and political development — and how they are, in turn, reshaped by markets, migration, and crises. My work combines large-scale historical data (newspapers, censuses, patents) with field experiments, spanning political economy, economic development, economic history, and cultural evolution.
My research has been published in the Journal of Political Economy and is forthcoming in the Journal of the European Economic Association. Some of my earlier work appeared under my former name, Max Winkler.

title: Research
text:
Publications

How Cultural Diversity Drives Innovation: Surnames and Patents in U.S. History

with Jonathan Schulz and Joseph Henrich · Journal of Political Economy, 2026, 134(4): 1245–1305


Using a surname-based measure of cultural diversity in U.S. counties from 1850 to 1940, we show that rising diversity increased both the quantity and quality of innovation — by expanding the range of ideas available for recombination and fostering the social interactions that spread them.


PDF Journal Replication package Forbes



The Political Economy of Propaganda: Evidence from U.S. Newspapers

with Sebastian Ottinger · Journal of the European Economic Association, accepted


Can racial outrage in the media be manufactured by elites for political gain? Using high-frequency newspaper data from the late nineteenth-century U.S. South, we find evidence consistent with Democratic elites orchestrating a racist propaganda campaign through local newspapers — and benefiting from it at the polls.


PDF Replication package Broadstreet

title: Research
text:
Working papers

On the Importance of African Traditional Religion for Economic Behavior

with Lewis D. Butinda, Aimable A. Lameke, Nathan Nunn, and Raul Sanchez de la Sierra · Reject & resubmit, Econometrica


Beer sellers in the eastern DRC overestimate the risk of theft and hold too little inventory as a result. Randomly-timed access to commonly-used protective rituals corrects these beliefs among sellers who believe in their efficacy — raising inventories, sales, and profits.


PDF BFI research summary



Doux Commerce: Markets, Culture, and Cooperation in 1850–1920 U.S.

with Itzchak Tzachi Raz


As railroads integrated American markets between 1850 and 1920, counties gaining market access developed more universalist, tolerant, and trusting cultures — with more impersonal cooperation and less reliance on kin-based support.


PDF Marginal Revolution National Affairs



Do Disasters Affect the Tightness of Social Norms?

New draft coming soon


Combining data on conflicts, epidemics, and natural and economic disasters with global survey data, I show that disasters tighten social norms — an effect that can persist for decades and is transmitted to the next generation.

title: Teaching
text:
Economics of Culture and Institutions (BEE3073)
This course uses a historical and political economy approach to study the evolution and comparative development of societies, focusing on the role of domestic institutions and culture.
Intermediate Microeconomics (BEE2025)
This undergraduate-level course is part one of a two-part series covering the foundations of microeconomics. It focuses on the consumer side of the economy (the theory of the consumer and pure exchange economies).
